Abstract
For a simple graph G with adjacency matrix A(G), let π(G, x) :=
per(xI −A(G)) be its permanental polynomial with roots µ1, . . . , µn ∈
C, and define the permanental energy Eper(G) := Pn
i=1 |µi|. We prove
a sharp universal lower bound: for every m-edge graph G, Eper(G) ≥
2√m, with equality if and only if G is a star together with isolated
vertices. We also prove the general upper bound Eper(G) ≤nρ(G),
where ρ(G) is the spectral radius, and we study Eper(G) on several
graph families.
Keywords. permanental polynomial, graph energy, extremal graph theory,
permanent

Introduced by Gutman [9], E(G) has become a central invariant in spectral
graph theory and mathematical chemistry.
Its original motivation comes
from the Hückel molecular orbital (HMO) model, where eigenvalues of molec-
ular graphs are used to approximate the total π-electron energy of conjugated

hydrocarbons; see [14]. More generally, spectral quantities such as E(G) pro-
vide concise descriptors of graph structure; see [5] for background on graph
spectra.
A bridge from linear algebra to graph invariants is via the characteristic
polynomial
χ(G, x) = det(xI −A(G)),
whose roots are exactly the eigenvalues λ1, . . . , λn. Since the determinant
can be computed in O(nω) arithmetic operations, where ω is the matrix-
multiplication exponent [4], this bridge is useful not only conceptually but
also computationally.
In particular, invariants such as E(G) have a rich
theory and admit efficient computation.

The only difference is
the sign factor, yet the consequences are dramatic.
Valiant proved that
computing per(M) is #P-complete, even for 0–1 matrices [26], making the
permanent a central object in theoretical computer science.
The Pólya Permanent Problem [23] asks when the permanent of a ma-
trix can be transformed into the determinant of a related matrix by suitable
sign changes. McCuaig [19] showed that this problem is equivalent to sev-
eral combinatorial and graph-theoretic problems, including counting perfect
matchings in a graph. This motivates studying which structural and spec-
tral properties are shared by the permanent and determinant, despite the
hardness of the permanent.
Analogous to the characteristic polynomial, the permanental polynomial
of a graph G is
π(G, x) := per(xI −A(G)).
Introduced by Turner [25], π(G, x) has been studied as a permanent-based
spectral invariant in graph theory and chemical graph theory; see [12, 20].
In particular, its coefficients and zeros have been used as structural de-
scriptors and computed for several chemically motivated families. Because
computing permanents is hard in general, much of the literature focuses on
structural properties and efficient computation for special graph families;
see [10, 11, 15]. Computational studies suggest that copermanental graphs
2


(nonisomorphic graphs with the same permanental polynomial) are rare, es-
pecially compared with cospectrality for the characteristic polynomial, so
π(G, x) may be a strong isomorphism heuristic [17]. Related work develops
the theory of permanental spectra [16, 22, 27].
Permanental energy. Let µ1, . . . , µn be the roots of π(G, x) (in general
µi ∈C), and write |µi| for their modulus. We define the permanental energy
of G as
Eper(G) =

|µi|.
Thus Eper(G) is a single number that summarizes the permanental roots,
in the same spirit as the usual graph energy. However, permanental roots
are often complex, so many standard eigenvalue techniques do not apply.
Notably, Dehmer et al. [6] studied graph descriptors built from the moduli
|µi| like P
i |µi| (that is, Eper(G)), P
i |µi|2, and more generally P
i |µi|p for
various p, and reported that these quantities empirically distinguish networks
well in practice. However, to the best of our knowledge, little general theory
is known for such modulus-based permanental descriptors.
Since computing the permanent is #P-complete, exactly computing π(G, x)
and its roots is infeasible in general; consequently, one should not expect effi-
cient exact computation of Eper(G) for arbitrary graphs. This makes general
bounds and extremal characterizations especially valuable, because they pro-
vide information about Eper(G) without requiring explicit root computation.
Despite the hardness of computing π(G, x) exactly, the quantity Eper(G)
admits sharp universal extremal behavior. We prove that among all graphs
with m edges, the minimum possible permanental energy is exactly 2√m,
attained only by a star plus isolated vertices. We prove the general upper
bound Eper(G) ≤nρ(G) and derive basic corollaries (Theorem 3.5 and Corol-
laries 3.6–3.7). We also give sharper information for several graph families,
in Section 4.
The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces
the necessary definitions, notations, and preliminary results. Section 3 proves
upper and lower bounds on Eper(G) and characterizes the extremal graphs.
Section 4 studies Eper(G) for several graph families. Section 5 lists future
directions, and the appendix contains proofs deferred from the main text.

3.2
Upper bounds
For a square matrix M, let ρ(M) be its spectral radius, that is, the largest
absolute value among its eigenvalues. In particular, for a graph G, we write
ρ(G) := ρ(A(G)). We use a standard bound of Brenner and Brualdi [3] on
the roots of per(xI −A) to upper bound Eper(G).
Lemma 3.4 (Brenner–Brualdi [3]). Let A ≥0 be an n × n matrix. Every
root µ of per(xI −A) satisfies |µ| ≤ρ(A).
Theorem 3.5. Let G be a simple graph on n vertices with spectral radius
ρ = ρ(G). Then
Eper(G) ≤nρ.
Proof. Let µ1, . . . , µn be the roots of π(G, x) = per(xI−A(G)). By Lemma 3.4
(applied to A(G) ≥0), we have |µi| ≤ρ for all i. Summing gives Eper(G) ≤
nρ.
Thus, any upper bound on ρ(G) immediately yields a corresponding up-
per bound on Eper(G) via Theorem 3.5.

Special families
In this section we discuss graph families for which Eper(G) admits sharper
information than the universal bounds of Section 3.
4.1
Bipartite families
For some bipartite graph classes, the permanental polynomial can be written
in terms of the characteristic polynomial of an associated matrix. This can
force Eper(G) to coincide with the usual adjacency energy E(G) and can also
yield stronger upper bounds for such classes.
If G is bipartite and has no cycle whose length is divisible by 4, then
Borowiecki [2] proved the following relation between the permanental and
characteristic polynomials.
Theorem 4.1. If G is bipartite and contains no cycle of length 4k for any
k ≥1, then
π(G, x) = i−nχ(G, ix).

Corollary 4.2. If G is bipartite and contains no cycle of length 4k for any
k ≥1, then Eper(G) = E(G).
Proof. By Theorem 4.1, the permanental roots are {−iλj}n
j=1 (with multi-

An orientation assigns a direction to each edge. Since G is bipartite,
every cycle of G has even length. We say that a cycle is oddly oriented in
an orientation σ if, when traversing the cycle, an odd number of its edges
are directed along the traversal. Given an orientation Gσ, let S(Gσ) be the
matrix with Suv = 1 if u →v is an arc of Gσ, Suv = −1 if v →u is an
arc, and Suv = 0 otherwise.

an orientation in which every cycle is oddly oriented, then the permanental
polynomial has an exact determinantal description.

5
Future Directions
Several interesting questions remain open. On the algorithmic side, it would
be interesting to determine the complexity of computing Eper(G) exactly, and
more realistically to understand the complexity of approximating Eper(G)
within additive error εn or relative error 1 ± ε. On the extremal side, our
general upper bound Eper(G) ≤nρ(G) is often not tight; finding universal
upper bounds that improve on this in nontrivial regimes seems particularly
worthwhile. Structurally, beyond the bipartite classes in Section 4, it remains
to characterize broad graph families for which Eper(G) = E(G), or to identify
clear obstructions to equality.
Finally, developing general constraints on
the location and multiplicity pattern of permanental roots (forced zeros,
symmetry, stability phenomena, etc.)
could provide new ways to control
Eper(G) without explicitly computing permanental roots.

Abstract: For a simple graph G with adjacency matrix A(G), let π(G, x) := per(xI −A(G)) be its permanental polynomial with roots µ1, . . . , µn ∈ C, and define the permanental energy Eper(G) := Pn i=1 |µi|. We prove a sharp universal lower bound: for every m-edge graph G, Eper(G) ≥ 2√m, with equality if and only if G is a star together with isolated vertices. We also prove the general upper bound Eper(G) ≤nρ(G), where ρ(G) is the spectral radius, and we study Eper(G) on several graph families.
